label: The final cause comes before the motor cause in explaining nature
claim: Of the causes at work in the generation of natural things, the final cause (the end or purpose) is prior to the motor cause, in nature as in art.
quote: Plainly, however, that cause is the first which we call the final one. For this is the Reason, and the Reason forms the starting-point, alike in the works of art and in works of nature.
scope: all works of nature, including animals and their parts
candidate_data: none known

label: The vertebrae are not formed by accidental breaking of the foetal backbone
claim: The division of the backbone into vertebrae is not, as Empedocles held, the result of the backbone being broken by the contorted position of the foetus in the womb, nor are animal characters in general mere incidents of development.
quote: Empedocles, then, was in error when he said that many of the characters presented by animals were merely the results of incidental occurrences during their development; for instance, that the backbone was divided as it is into vertebrae, because it happened to be broken owing to the contorted position of the foetus in the womb.
measurable_quantities: timing of vertebral segmentation relative to foetal posture
presence of vertebral segmentation in embryos before mechanical loading
candidate_data: Embryological staging series and developmental-anatomy ontologies (e.g. Uberon, ZFIN staging for zebrafish) documenting when vertebral segments form.

label: Like begets like: the parent's characters determine the offspring's
claim: Man is generated from man, and it is the possession of certain characters by the parent that determines the development of like characters in the offspring.
quote: For man is generated from man; and thus it is the possession of certain characters by the parent that determines the development of like characters in the child.
scope: all animals that are generated from parents, with man as the example
measurable_quantities: parent–offspring resemblance in traits
candidate_data: Parent–offspring trait regressions and heritability estimates compiled in quantitative-genetics literature and animal-breeding databases.

label: Only man has intellect, though other animals move themselves
claim: Other animals besides man have the power of locomotion, but none but man has intellect.
quote: I say not the intellectual part; for other animals than man have the power of locomotion, but in none but him is there intellect.
scope: all animals, man contrasted with the rest
measurable_quantities: performance of non-human animals on reasoning and problem-solving tasks
candidate_data: Comparative cognition test batteries and published primate and corvid problem-solving studies; no single standard database known.

label: Respiration is driven by an alternation of heat and cooling
claim: Breathing exists for the alternate discharge and re-entry of heat, and the alternation of heating and cooling in the body necessarily produces the alternate intake and discharge of outer air.
quote: For the alternate discharge and re-entrance of heat and the inflow of air are necessary if we are to live. Here we have at once a necessity in the former of the two senses. But the alternation of heat and refrigeration produces of necessity an alternate admission and discharge of the outer air, and this is a necessity of the second kind.
measurable_quantities: temperature of inspired versus expired air
whether ventilation rate tracks body heat or tracks gas-exchange demand
candidate_data: Respiratory physiology measurements of ventilation, expired-air temperature and ventilatory control in mammals.

label: Groups such as Wild and Tame cannot divide species, since tame kinds also occur wild
claim: In almost all kinds of animal of which some members are tame, other members are wild, so wildness and tameness are not specific differences.
quote: For in almost all species in which some members are tame, there are other members that are wild. Such, for example, is the case with Men, Horses, Oxen, Dogs in India, Pigs, Goats, Sheep
scope: domesticated animals: horse, ox, dog, pig, goat, sheep, and man
measurable_quantities: existence of wild or feral populations of the same kind as each domesticated animal
candidate_data: Domestication records and wild-progenitor taxonomy (e.g. GBIF occurrences of wild and feral populations, the Animal Diversity Web).

label: Some ants fly and others do not
claim: Among ants some fly and others do not, so Flying versus Walking cannot be used to divide animal kinds.
quote: For some groups, Ants for instance, fall under both divisions, some ants flying while others do not.
measurable_quantities: presence of winged and wingless individuals within ant species
candidate_data: Ant caste and morphology data in AntWeb and AntWiki, and the Animal Diversity Web.

label: Natural groups are marked by many differentiae, not by dichotomy
claim: Animals should be classified into the natural groups that mankind instinctively recognizes, such as Birds and Fishes, each defined by many differentiae together, and not by successive two-way division on a single character.
quote: The method then that we must adopt is to attempt to recognize the natural groups, following the indications afforded by the instincts of mankind, which led them for instance to form the class of Birds and the class of Fishes, each of which groups combines a multitude of differentiae, and is not defined by a single one as in dichotomy.
candidate_data: none known

label: Within a class animals differ by degree; across classes their parts are only analogous
claim: Animals within one class differ only by degree (more and less of the same part), while different classes agree only in having analogous organs, as the bird's feather corresponds to the fish's scale.
quote: For instance, bird differs from bird by gradation, or by excess and defect; some birds have long feathers, others short ones, but all are feathered. Bird and Fish are more remote and only agree in having analogous organs; for what in the bird is feather, in the fish is scale.
scope: birds and fishes as examples of classes
measurable_quantities: correspondence of feathers and fish scales in structure and development
candidate_data: Comparative integument anatomy and homology annotations in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase.

label: Groups lacking lungs or blood have analogous organs and fluids in their place
claim: Some groups of animals have lungs and others have instead an organ analogous to a lung; some have blood and others have instead a fluid analogous to blood with the same office.
quote: For instance, some groups have lungs, others have no lung, but an organ analogous to a lung in its place; some have blood, others have no blood, but a fluid analogous to blood, and with the same office.
scope: all animals: lunged versus unlunged, animals with blood versus bloodless animals
measurable_quantities: presence of lungs or other respiratory organs across taxa
presence of a circulating fluid in animals Aristotle calls bloodless
candidate_data: Comparative anatomy in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase; the Animal Diversity Web.

label: The body exists for the soul and each part for its function
claim: As each instrument serves some action, the body is made for the soul and each part of the body for some subordinate function to which it is adapted.
quote: Thus the saw is made for sawing, for sawing is a function, and not sawing for the saw. Similarly, the body too must somehow or other be made for the soul, and each part of it for some subordinate function, to which it is adapted.
candidate_data: none known

label: Homogeneous tissues exist for the sake of the heterogeneous organs
claim: Animals are composed of homogeneous parts (such as bone and flesh) and heterogeneous parts (such as face and hand), and the homogeneous parts exist for the sake of the heterogeneous ones, which carry on the body's functions.
quote: Animals, then, are composed of homogeneous parts, and are also composed of heterogeneous parts. The former, however, exist for the sake of the latter. For the active functions and operations of the body are carried on by these; that is, by the heterogeneous parts, such as the eye, the nostril, the whole face, the fingers, the hand, and the whole arm.
candidate_data: none known

label: The heart is the seat of sensation, motion and nutrition in blooded animals
claim: The sensory, motor and nutritive faculties are lodged in one central part, which in animals with blood is the heart and in bloodless animals the part that takes the place of a heart.
quote: For this reason it is the heart which in sanguineous animals constitutes this central part, and in bloodless animals it is that which takes the place of a heart.
scope: animals with blood (roughly vertebrates) and bloodless animals
measurable_quantities: effect of heart versus brain lesions on sensation and voluntary movement
candidate_data: Neurophysiology and lesion studies; heart-transplant and artificial-heart patient outcomes in the clinical literature.

label: Thick hot blood gives strength; thin cool blood gives sensation and intelligence
claim: The thicker and hotter an animal's blood, the more it conduces to strength; the thinner and colder, the better suited it is to sensation and intelligence; those with hot, thin and clear blood are best for both courage and intelligence.
quote: As regards the results of such differences, the thicker and the hotter blood is, the more conducive is it to strength, while in proportion to its thinness and its coldness is its suitability for sensation and intelligence.
scope: animals with blood, and by analogy bloodless animals
measurable_quantities: blood viscosity or haematocrit
body temperature
measures of strength and of cognitive performance across species
candidate_data: Comparative haematology (e.g. species reference intervals in veterinary literature), AnAge and body-temperature compilations, comparative cognition studies.

label: Blood solidifies outside the body, yellow bile becomes more fluid
claim: Blood is hot and fluid in the living body but becomes cold and coagulates when separated from it, whereas yellow bile becomes more fluid when separated.
quote: Of the former blood is an example, of the latter bile; for while blood solidifies when thus separated, yellow bile under the same circumstances becomes more fluid.
measurable_quantities: clotting of shed blood
viscosity of bile after removal from the body
candidate_data: Clinical coagulation data and biliary physiology measurements of bile viscosity.

label: Nearly all animals, and all that move about, have a stomach
claim: Animals, with scarcely an exception and conspicuously all those capable of locomotion, have a stomach-sac that serves them as an internal substitute for the earth from which plants draw food.
quote: But animals, with scarcely an exception, and conspicuously all such as are capable of locomotion, are provided with a stomachal sac, which is as it were an internal substitute for the earth.
scope: all animals, especially those that move from place to place
measurable_quantities: presence of a stomach or gut sac across animal taxa
candidate_data: Comparative digestive anatomy in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase; the Animal Diversity Web.

label: Blood is the final nutriment and its quantity follows food intake
claim: Blood is the final nutritive material of the body in animals that have it; it diminishes in quantity when no food is taken, increases when much is eaten, and is healthy or unhealthy according to the food.
quote: This explains why the blood diminishes in quantity when no food is taken, and increases when much is consumed, and also why it becomes healthy and unhealthy according as the food is of the one or the other character.
scope: animals with blood; in bloodless animals the analogous fluid
measurable_quantities: blood volume during fasting versus feeding
blood composition in relation to diet
candidate_data: Physiological studies of blood volume and plasma composition under fasting and feeding in humans and laboratory animals.

label: Deer and roe blood has no fibres and never coagulates
claim: The blood of deer and of roe deer contains no fibres and for this reason never coagulates.
quote: There are none, for instance, in the blood of deer and of roes; and for this reason the blood of such animals as these never coagulates.
measurable_quantities: clotting time and fibrinogen concentration in cervid blood
candidate_data: Veterinary haematology reference values for cervids, e.g. Species360 ZIMS physiological reference intervals.

label: Bloodless animals are more timorous, freezing and discharging excretions when frightened
claim: Bloodless animals are, as a general rule, more timorous than animals with blood: when frightened they stay motionless, discharge their excretions and in some cases change colour.
quote: This also explains why bloodless animals are, as a general rule, more timorous than such as have blood, so that they remain motionless, when frightened, and discharge their excretions, and in some instances change colour.
scope: bloodless animals (invertebrates such as cephalopods and insects) compared with animals with blood
measurable_quantities: frequency of freezing, ink or excretion discharge and colour change as fear responses
candidate_data: Behavioural ecology literature on defensive behaviour in cephalopods and arthropods; the Animal Diversity Web.

label: Bull's blood coagulates faster than any other animal's
claim: Bulls and boars have blood exceedingly rich in fibres, and the bull's blood coagulates more rapidly than that of any other animal.
quote: This explains why bulls and boars are so choleric and so passionate. For their blood is exceedingly rich in fibres, and the bull's at any rate coagulates more rapidly than that of any other animal.
scope: bulls (Bos taurus) and boars (Sus scrofa), compared with all other animals
measurable_quantities: clotting time of bovine blood compared with other species
fibrinogen concentration in cattle and pigs
candidate_data: Comparative veterinary coagulation studies and species haematology reference intervals.

label: Horned animals lacking upper front teeth have suet; others have lard
claim: Horned animals without front teeth in the upper jaw have fat in the form of suet, whereas hornless animals with front teeth in both jaws and toed feet have lard, which neither coagulates nor dries into a friable mass.
quote: Thus it is that in those horned animals that have no front teeth in the upper jaw the fat consists of suet.
scope: horned animals without upper incisors (ruminants such as ox, sheep, goat) versus hornless animals with incisors in both jaws (such as pig)
measurable_quantities: melting point and saturation of body fat in ruminants versus non-ruminants
candidate_data: Animal fat composition data in food-composition tables (e.g. USDA FoodData Central) and lipid chemistry literature.

label: Fat animals are less prolific
claim: Fat animals are less prolific than others, because the blood that should form semen is used up in making lard and suet.
quote: For the same reason fat animals are less prolific than others. For that part of the blood which should go to form semen and seed is used up in the production of lard and suet
measurable_quantities: fertility or litter size in relation to body fat within species
candidate_data: Livestock reproduction studies relating body condition to fertility, and human epidemiology of obesity and fertility.

label: The lion's bones have almost no marrow
claim: Animals with strong and solid bones, such as the lion, have hardly any marrow, the lion's being so insignificant that its bones look as though they had none.
quote: There are some animals that can hardly be said to have any marrow. These are those whose bones are strong and solid, as is the case with the lion. For in this animal the marrow is so utterly insignificant that the bones look as though they had none at all.
scope: lion (Panthera leo) and other animals with strong compact bones
measurable_quantities: medullary cavity size and marrow content in lion long bones compared with other mammals
candidate_data: CT scans of carnivore skeletons in MorphoSource and comparative cortical-bone thickness studies.

label: The brain is the coldest part of the body and bloodless in its substance
claim: Of all parts of the body none is as cold as the brain, which is cold to the touch and has no blood in its proper substance.
quote: The coldness of the brain is also manifest enough. For in the first place it is cold even to the touch; and, secondly, of all the fluid parts of the body it is the driest and the one that has the least blood; for in fact it has no blood at all in its proper substance.
measurable_quantities: brain temperature relative to other organs
cerebral blood flow and vascularity
candidate_data: Human and animal brain-temperature measurements and cerebral blood flow data in physiology literature.

label: The brain exists to cool the heat of the heart
claim: Nature has made the brain, a compound of earth and water, as a counterpoise to the heat of the region of the heart, to moderate it.
quote: nature has contrived the brain as a counterpoise to the region of the heart with its contained heat, and has given it to animals to moderate the latter, combining in it the properties of earth and water.
measurable_quantities: contribution of the brain to cooling the blood or heart
brain metabolic heat production
candidate_data: Thermal physiology studies of brain heat production and selective brain cooling in mammals.

label: Every animal with blood has a brain; no bloodless animal has one
claim: Every animal with blood has a brain, whereas no bloodless animal has such an organ, except by analogy, as in the poulp (octopus).
quote: For this reason it is, that every sanguineous animal has a brain; whereas no bloodless creature has such an organ, unless indeed it be, as the Poulp, by analogy.
scope: animals with blood (roughly vertebrates) versus bloodless animals (invertebrates), with the poulp (octopus) as exception
measurable_quantities: presence of a brain or cerebral ganglia across animal taxa
candidate_data: Comparative neuroanatomy in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase; invertebrate neuroanatomy literature.

label: The brain causes sleep by chilling the blood rising after food
claim: The brain, or its analogue, is the cause of sleep: by chilling the blood that streams upward after food it produces heaviness in the head and drives the heat downward with the blood.
quote: It is the brain again-or, in animals that have no brain, the part analogous to it-which is the cause of sleep. For either by chilling the blood that streams upwards after food, or by some other similar influences, it produces heaviness in the region in which it lies
measurable_quantities: role of the brain in initiating sleep
post-meal drowsiness and blood flow
candidate_data: Sleep neuroscience literature on brain sleep-regulating circuits and postprandial somnolence.

label: Man has the largest brain for his size, and men larger than women
claim: Of all animals, man has the largest brain in proportion to his size, and the brain is larger in men than in women.
quote: Of all animals, man has the largest brain in proportion to his size; and it is larger in men than in women.
scope: man compared with all other animals; men compared with women
measurable_quantities: brain mass relative to body mass across species
brain mass in men and women, absolute and relative to body size
candidate_data: Comparative brain and body mass compilations (e.g. published mammal and bird brain-size datasets), PanTHERIA body masses, and human neuroimaging cohorts such as the UK Biobank.

label: Only in man does the bregma solidify last
claim: In man the cranial bone called the bregma is the last to become solidified, because evaporation continues through it under the influence of heat; man is the only animal with blood in which this happens.
quote: it is again owing to this superabundance that the cranial bone, which some call the Bregma, is the last to become solidified; so long does evaporation continue to occur through it under the influence of heat. Man is the only sanguineous animal in which this takes place.
scope: man compared with other animals with blood
measurable_quantities: age at closure of the anterior fontanelle in humans and other mammals
candidate_data: Comparative cranial ontogeny studies and skull CT collections in MorphoSource.

label: Man has more skull sutures than any animal, males more than females
claim: Man has more sutures in his skull than any other animal, and the male more than the female, because the larger brain requires more ventilation.
quote: Man, again, has more sutures in his skull than any other animal, and the male more than the female.
scope: man compared with other animals; men compared with women
measurable_quantities: number of cranial sutures by species and by sex
candidate_data: Comparative cranial anatomy and skull CT collections in MorphoSource; Uberon for suture inventories.

label: Crustaceans and testaceans have their hard supporting part outside
claim: In all crustaceans and testaceans the fleshy substance is within and the hard earthy matter is outside, and the shell both holds the soft parts together and keeps in their scanty natural heat.
quote: For in all these animals the fleshy substance is within, and the earthy matter, which holds the soft parts together and keeps them from injury, is on the outside. For the shell not only enables the soft parts to hold together, but also, as the animal is bloodless and so has but little natural warmth, surrounds it
scope: crustaceans (crabs, spiny lobsters) and testaceans (shelled molluscs such as oysters)
measurable_quantities: presence of an exoskeleton or shell
heat retention by shells
candidate_data: Comparative invertebrate anatomy in the Animal Diversity Web and SeaLifeBase; thermal biology studies of shelled invertebrates.

label: Cuttlefish and squid have an internal shell; the octopus has none
claim: Cuttlefishes have an internal hard part (the os sepiae) and calamaries (squids) the gladius, but poulps (octopuses) have no such part because their body-sac is short.
quote: For instance, in the Cuttle-fishes there is what is known as the os sepiae, and in the Calamaries there is the so-called gladius. In the Poulps, on the other hand, there is no such internal part
measurable_quantities: presence of cuttlebone, gladius or internal shell remnant
mantle length
candidate_data: Cephalopod anatomy in SeaLifeBase, the Tree of Life Web Project and the Animal Diversity Web.

label: The belly wall is boneless in all animals
claim: The walls of the belly are in all animals devoid of bones, so as not to hinder its expansion after a meal or the growth of the foetus in females.
quote: The walls of this are in all animals devoid of bones; in order that there may be no hindrance to the expansion which necessarily occurs in this part after a meal, nor, in females, any interference with the growth of the foetus, which is lodged here.
measurable_quantities: presence of bones (e.g. gastralia) in the abdominal wall across vertebrates
candidate_data: Comparative skeletal anatomy in Uberon, the Phenoscape Knowledgebase and MorphoSource specimens.

label: Males' bones are harder than females', carnivores' harder than herbivores'
claim: The bones of males are harder than those of females, and the bones of carnivores that get their food by fighting are harder than those of herbivores.
quote: Thus it is that the bones of males are harder than those of females; and the bones of flesh-eaters, that get their food by fighting, are harder than those of Herbivora.
measurable_quantities: bone mineral density or hardness by sex
bone mineral density in carnivores versus herbivores
candidate_data: Bone densitometry studies in mammals and comparative bone-material-property literature; EltonTraits for diet classification.

label: The lion's bones are so hard they give off sparks when struck
claim: The lion's bones are so hard that when struck they give off sparks, as though they were stones.
quote: Of this the Lion is an example; for so hard are its bones, that, when struck, they give off sparks, as though they were stones.
measurable_quantities: hardness of lion bone
whether bone produces sparks when struck
candidate_data: Bone material-property measurements; none specific to lions known.

label: The dolphin, being viviparous, has bones rather than fish-spines
claim: The dolphin, being viviparous, has bones and not fish-spines.
quote: It may be mentioned also that the Dolphin, in as much as it is viviparous, is provided with bones and not with fish-spines.
measurable_quantities: skeletal tissue type in dolphins
candidate_data: Cetacean skeletal anatomy in MorphoSource and the Animal Diversity Web.

label: Selachians have cartilage instead of fish-spine, for undulating movement
claim: In selachians (cartilaginous fishes) the fish-spines are replaced by cartilage, because their undulating movement requires a pliable rather than brittle supporting framework.
quote: Lastly, in the Selachia, as they are called, the fish-spines are replaced by cartilage. For it is necessary that the movements of these animals shall be of an undulating character; and this again requires the framework that supports the body to be made of a pliable and not of a brittle substance.
measurable_quantities: skeletal tissue type in chondrichthyans
swimming mode of chondrichthyans
candidate_data: FishBase for chondrichthyan taxonomy and swimming mode; Uberon and Phenoscape for skeletal tissue annotations.

label: Neither cartilage nor bone grows again once cut off
claim: Cartilage and bone differ only in degree, and neither cartilage nor bone grows again once cut off.
quote: Cartilage and bone are indeed fundamentally the same thing, the differences between them being merely matters of degree. Thus neither cartilage nor bone, when once cut off, grows again.
measurable_quantities: regrowth of amputated bone or cartilage across taxa
candidate_data: Regeneration literature on limb, fin and antler regrowth in vertebrates.

label: The brain is insensible and not the cause of sensation
claim: The brain cannot be the cause of any sensation, being itself as without feeling as any of the excretions; the sensory centre is the region of the heart.
quote: and, as to the other half of their statement, the brain cannot be the cause of any of the sensations, seeing that it is itself as utterly without feeling as any one of the excretions.
measurable_quantities: pain response to touching brain tissue
effect of brain lesions on sensation
candidate_data: Neurosurgical observations of awake craniotomy and lesion studies in the clinical neuroscience literature.

label: Birds and scaly oviparous quadrupeds have no external ears
claim: Birds have no ears but only the auditory passages, because their skin is hard and they have feathers instead of hair; the same is true of oviparous quadrupeds clad in scaly plates.
quote: In birds, on the other hand, there are no ears, but only the auditory passages. This is because their skin is hard and because they have feathers instead of hairs, so that they have not got the proper material for the formation of ears.
measurable_quantities: presence of an external ear (pinna) across taxa
candidate_data: Comparative anatomy annotations for the pinna in Uberon and the Phenoscape Knowledgebase.

label: The seal has no external ears, only auditory passages
claim: The seal, alone among viviparous quadrupeds, has no ears but only the auditory passages, being a quadruped of stunted formation.
quote: There is also one of the viviparous quadrupeds, namely the seal, that has no ears but only the auditory passages. The explanation of this is that the seal, though a quadruped, is a quadruped of stunted formation.
measurable_quantities: presence of an external ear in seals and other mammals
candidate_data: Pinniped anatomy in the Animal Diversity Web; mammal trait compilations such as PanTHERIA for taxon coverage.

label: Some animals close the eye with the lower lid; birds blink with a membrane
claim: Viviparous animals have two eyelids and use both to close and to blink; oviparous quadrupeds and heavy-bodied birds close the eye with the lower lid only, while birds blink with a membrane issuing from the corner of the eye.
quote: whereas the oviparous quadrupeds, and the heavy-bodied birds as well as some others, use only the lower lid to close the eye; while birds blink by means of a membrane that issues from the canthus.
scope: viviparous animals (mammals), oviparous quadrupeds (reptiles), heavy-bodied birds (e.g. fowl) and birds generally
measurable_quantities: which eyelid closes the eye
presence and use of a nictitating membrane
candidate_data: Comparative ocular anatomy literature on eyelids and nictitating membranes in birds, reptiles and mammals.

label: Birds of prey are sharp-sighted, ground fowl are not
claim: Birds with talons, which search for prey by eye from aloft and soar higher than other birds, are sharp-sighted, while common fowls and similar ground-living birds have no such keenness of vision.
quote: This too explains why birds with talons, that have to search for prey by eye from aloft, and therefore soar to greater heights than other birds, are sharpsighted; while common fowls and the like, that live on the ground and are not made for flight, have no such keenness of vision.
scope: birds with talons (raptors) versus ground fowl (Galliformes)
measurable_quantities: visual acuity in raptors versus galliforms
candidate_data: Published comparative avian visual-acuity measurements; AVONET for ecological traits and lifestyle.

label: Fishes, insects and crustaceans have no eyelids
claim: Fishes, insects and hard-skinned crustaceans have no eyelids; insects and still more crustaceans compensate for their hard eyes by having movable eyes.
quote: Fishes and Insects and the hard-skinned Crustacea present certain differences in their eyes, but so far resemble each other as that none of them have eyelids.
measurable_quantities: presence of eyelids
mobility of the eyes (e.g. stalked eyes)
candidate_data: Comparative eye anatomy in Uberon, FishBase and arthropod morphology literature.

label: All hairy animals have eyelashes; birds and scaly animals lack them, except the ostrich
claim: All animals with hair on the body have eyelashes, while birds and animals with scaly plates, being hairless, have none; the Libyan ostrich is an exception, having eyelashes though a bird.
quote: All animals that have hairs on the body have lashes on the eyelids; but birds and animals with scale-like plates, being hairless, have none. The Libyan ostrich, indeed, forms an exception; for, though a bird, it is furnished with eyelashes.
scope: hairy animals (mammals), birds, scaly animals (reptiles), ostrich (Struthio camelus)
measurable_quantities: presence of eyelashes across taxa
candidate_data: Comparative integument studies of eyelashes in mammals and birds; the Animal Diversity Web.

label: Only man has lashes on both eyelids; no quadruped has a lower eyelash
claim: Of hairy animals, man alone has lashes on both eyelids; no quadruped has a lower eyelash, though some have a few scattered hairs under the lower lid.
quote: Of hairy animals, man alone has lashes on both lids.
measurable_quantities: presence of lower-lid lashes across mammal species
candidate_data: Comparative mammalian eyelash measurements in the published literature; museum specimen photographs.

label: The elephant uses its nostril as a hand
claim: The elephant's proboscis is a nostril which it uses as a hand, conveying food and drink to its mouth and tearing up trees by coiling it round their stems.
quote: For the elephant uses its nostril as a hand; this being the instrument with which it conveys food, fluid and solid alike, to its mouth. With it, too, it tears up trees, coiling it round their stems.
measurable_quantities: use of the trunk in feeding, drinking and uprooting vegetation
candidate_data: Elephant behavioural ecology studies and the Animal Diversity Web.

label: Elephants breathe through the raised trunk when crossing water
claim: Elephants, being both land and swamp animals, have a lengthened nostril which, when they traverse water, they lift above the surface and breathe through, like a diver's breathing instrument.
quote: so also have elephants been furnished by nature with their lengthened nostril; and, whenever they have to traverse the water, they lift this up above the surface and breathe through it.
measurable_quantities: snorkelling with the trunk during swimming
time spent in water
candidate_data: Field observations of elephant swimming behaviour and the Animal Diversity Web.

label: Birds that pronounce letters best have the broadest tongues
claim: Among birds, those most capable of pronouncing letters have the broadest tongues, whereas viviparous quadrupeds, whose tongue is hard, thick and not free, have very limited vocal articulation.
quote: What has been said explains why, among birds, those that are most capable of pronouncing letters are such as have the broadest tongues; and why the viviparous and sanguineous quadrupeds, where the tongue is hard and thick and not free in its motions, have a very limited vocal articulation.
scope: birds (especially talking birds such as parrots) and viviparous quadrupeds (mammals)
measurable_quantities: tongue breadth
capacity for vocal imitation of human speech
candidate_data: Comparative studies of vocal mimicry in parrots and other birds, with tongue morphology from museum specimens; AVONET for taxon coverage.

label: All birds communicate with their tongues, some seeming to teach one another
claim: All birds use their tongues to communicate with each other, some more than others, so that in some cases it seems as though actual instruction passes from one bird to another.
quote: All birds use their tongues to communicate with each other. But some do this in a greater degree than the rest; so that in some cases it even seems as though actual instruction were imparted from one to another by its agency.
measurable_quantities: prevalence of vocal communication across bird species
occurrence of vocal learning from tutors
candidate_data: Song-learning and vocal-learning literature, xeno-canto recordings, and AVONET for taxon coverage.

label: Serpents and lizards have long forked tongues suited to taste
claim: Land-dwelling oviparous animals with blood mostly have a tongue tied down and hard, but in serpents and lizards it is long and forked, suiting it to the perception of savours.
quote: As to those oviparous and sanguineous animals that live not in the air but on the earth, their tongue in most cases is tied down and hard, and is therefore useless for vocal purposes; in the serpents, however, and in the lizards it is long and forked, so as to be suited for the perception of savours.
scope: terrestrial oviparous animals with blood (reptiles, amphibians), especially snakes and lizards
measurable_quantities: tongue length and degree of forking
role of the tongue in chemical sensing
candidate_data: Squamate tongue morphology and chemoreception studies; The Reptile Database for taxon coverage.

label: The crocodile moves its upper jaw and its tongue adheres to the lower
claim: The crocodile's tongue is adherent to the lower jaw, which is immobile; in the crocodile it is the upper jaw that moves, the reverse of other animals.
quote: For the crocodile's tongue is adherent to the lower jaw. For its upper and lower jaws are, as it were, inverted, it being the upper jaw which in other animals is the immovable one.
measurable_quantities: which jaw moves during feeding
attachment of the tongue to the floor of the mouth
candidate_data: Crocodilian skull and jaw-mechanics studies, MorphoSource skull scans and The Reptile Database.

label: Purple snails bore through shells with their tongue
claim: In the purpurae (purple snails) the tongue-like part is so strong that it bores holes through the shells of other shellfish, such as the spiral snails used as bait to catch them.
quote: In the Purpurae, for instance, so strong is this part that it enables them to bore holes through the hard covering of shell-fish, of the spiral snails, for example, that are used as bait to catch them.
scope: purpurae (murex and related purple-dye snails, Muricidae)
measurable_quantities: drilling of prey shells by muricid gastropods
candidate_data: Predatory drill-hole studies in marine gastropods, SeaLifeBase and WoRMS for taxon coverage, and the Paleobiology Database for fossil drill holes.
